Abstract 
Emotion recognition in dynamic and real-world environments presents significant 
challenges due to the complexity and variability of multimodal data. This paper intro-
duces an innovative Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) framework that seam-
lessly integrates text, audio, video, and motion data using advanced machine learning 
techniques. To address challenges such as class imbalance, the framework employs 
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for synthetic sample generation and Dynamic 
Prompt Engineering (DPE) for enhanced feature extraction across modalities. Text 
features are processed with Mistral-7B, audio with HuBERT, video with TimeSformer 
and LLaVA, and motion with MediaPipe Pose. The system efficiently fuses these inputs 
using Hierarchical Attention-based Graph Neural Networks (HAN-GNN) and Cross-
Modality Transformer Fusion (XMTF), further improved by contrastive learning 
with Prototypical Networks to enhance class separation. The framework demonstrates 
exceptional performance, achieving training accuracies of 99.92% on IEMOCAP 
and 99.95% on MELD, with testing accuracies of 99.82% and 99.81%, respectively. High 
precision, recall, and specificity further highlight the robustness of the model. While 
trained on batch-processed datasets, the framework has been optimized for real-time 
applications, demonstrating computational efficiency with training completed in just 
5 min and inference times under 0.4 ms per sample. This makes the system well-
suited for real-time emotion recognition tasks despite being trained on batch data. It 
also generalizes effectively to noisy and multilingual settings, achieving strong results 
on SAVEE and CMU-MOSEAS, thereby confirming its resilience in diverse real-world 
scenarios. This research advances the field of MER, offering a scalable and efficient 
solution for affective computing. The findings emphasize the importance of refining 
these systems for real-world applications, particularly in complex, multimodal big data 
environments.

Introduction
Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) integrates data from text, audio, video, and 
motion to enable systems to interpret human emotions with greater accuracy and 
robustness compared to unimodal approaches [1]. By combining complementary cues 
across modalities, MER addresses the limitations of single-modality systems, captur-
ing nuanced emotional expressions in diverse contexts such as social media, virtual 
assistants, and human-robot interaction [2].
Emotion recognition is a cornerstone of human-computer interaction, enabling sys-
tems to detect and respond to human affect, thereby enhancing user experiences in 
domains like healthcare, education, and entertainment [3]. The importance of MER 
lies in its ability to leverage diverse data sources to overcome challenges like envi-
ronmental noise and missing contextual cues, making it critical for real-world appli-
cations where big data introduces complexities such as modality misalignment and 
linguistic diversity [4]. Despite advancements, MER systems face significant chal-
lenges in cross-modal alignment, static fusion mechanisms, and robustness to noise, 
data imbalance, and multilingual variability, limiting real-time applicability [5].
Research gap and motivation
Current MER approaches rely on early or late fusion strategies, lacking mechanisms 
to model complex temporal dynamics, inter-modal interactions, and speaker variabil-
ity [6, 7]. These limitations, coupled with challenges in handling noisy, imbalanced, 
and multilingual data, hinder generalization across diverse scenarios [8]. Advancing 
MER is motivated by the need for accurate emotion detection in applications like 
healthcare, customer service, and human-robot interaction, where addressing the fol-
lowing is critical:
•	 Modality Misalignment: Variations in data capture rates and sources complicate 
fusion.
•	 Data Imbalance: Underrepresented emotions lead to biased predictions.
•	 Complex and Multilingual Expression: Nuanced and language-specific cues 
require adaptive techniques.
To address these challenges, this work proposes a unified, end-to-end framework that 
integrates advanced modality-specific encoding, context-aware fusion, and strategic 
data augmentation
Contributions and innovations
This framework introduces the following innovations: 
1.	 Cross-Modality Representation: Employs HuBERT (audio), Mistral-7B (text), 
TimeSformer and LLaVA (video), and MediaPipe (motion) for modality-aligned fea-
ture extraction, enabling high-quality, context-sensitive emotion representations.

Related work
Advancements in Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) from 2023 to 2025 have lev-
eraged deep learning to integrate text, audio, video, and motion, addressing complex 
emotional expressions as reviewed by Zhao et al. [1]. Despite progress, theoretical chal-
lenges in cross-modal dependency modeling, temporal dynamics, and generalizability 
under noise and cultural diversity persist, alongside empirical limitations in real-world

Unimodal emotion recognition
Unimodal approaches laid the foundation for emotion recognition, focusing on single 
modalities like speech or text. Aguilera et al. [9] emphasized dataset diversity to capture 
subtle emotions, yet unimodal systems struggled with missing complementary cues, as 
presented by Shepard et al. [6]. Tellia et al. [10] proposed a dual-level Speech Emotion 
Recognition (SER) system using MFCCs and Mel-spectrograms with hierarchical atten-
tion, achieving 75.9% unweighted accuracy on IEMOCAP. This approach, grounded 
in local feature extraction, lacks cross-modal interaction modeling—a theoretical gap 
addressed by the proposed framework’s modality-aligned encoders (HuBERT, Mistral-
7B, TimeSformer), which integrate complementary cues for enhanced expressiveness.
Early multimodal fusion approaches
Early multimodal systems combined modalities through simplistic fusion. Makhmudov 
et al. [11] integrated speech and text, achieving 88.4% accuracy on CMU-MOSEI, but 
rigid early fusion limited robustness to noise. Subsequently, Bilotti et al. [12] used CNN-
based fusion of facial frames and Mel spectrograms, reaching 95% accuracy in controlled 
settings but degrading in dynamic environments due to static modality weighting. 
These empirical limitations in environmental adaptability are mitigated by the proposed 
framework’s Cross-Modality Transformer Fusion (XMTF) and Hierarchical Attention-
Based GNN (HAN-GNN), which dynamically balance modalities and model structural 
dependencies.
Advanced fusion and dependency modeling
Recent studies advanced fusion through inter-modal modeling. Zhang et al. [13] pro-
posed MER-HAN, enhancing attention mechanisms but struggling with data imbalance 
for underrepresented emotions. Shou et al. [14] introduced AGF-IB, achieving 70.46% 
weighted accuracy on IEMOCAP, yet limited by static feature extraction for nuanced 
emotions. Zhu et  al.  [15] developed RMER-DT, a diffusion- and transformer-based 
model, achieving 72.03% WAA on IEMOCAP and 67.85% on MELD, excelling in subtle 
emotion detection but constrained by limited temporal abstraction in long dialogues. In 
another view, Wang et al. [16] proposed RAFT, achieving over 80% binary accuracy on 
MOSI and MOSEI with robust noise resilience but lacking cultural variation modeling. 
These theoretical gaps in temporal and inter-modal dependency modeling are addressed 
by the proposed framework’s HAN-GNN for structural dependencies and contrastive 
learning for emotion class separation.
Real‑time and scalable MER systems
Recent efforts focused on real-time and scalable MER. Jena et al. [17] combined CNNs 
and LSTMs, achieving 94.6% accuracy in controlled settings but degrading under 
domain shifts. Fu et al. [18] proposed HiMul-LGG, reaching 92% on MELD but drop-
ping to 85% during emotional transitions due to weak temporal modeling. Ma et al. [8]

•	 Scalability and Robustness: Enhances the generalizability of MER systems,

Data preprocessing
The preprocessing phase [61] is critical for ensuring consistency, quality, and cross-
modal alignment in MER. Given the heterogeneous nature of textual, acoustic, visual, 
and motion-based data, dedicated preprocessing techniques are applied to each modal-

normalization procedures are further employed to mitigate discrepancies arising from 
diverse data distributions.
The preprocessing strategy is designed to address challenges associated with big data 
variety, ensuring compatibility across different modalities. The key objectives include:
•	 Standardization and Normalization: Variability in text embeddings, audio sampling 
rates, video frame resolutions, and motion capture sequences necessitates standardi-
zation to ensure consistency.
•	 Noise Reduction and Data Cleaning: Removal of redundant information, such 
as background noise in audio, blurred frames in video, or irrelevant text tokens, 
enhances feature discriminability.
•	 Temporal Synchronization: Alignment of modalities with different temporal resolu-
tions is critical for accurate emotion recognition.
•	 Computational Efficiency: High-dimensional raw data is optimized through feature 
selection and dimensionality reduction techniques.

Data augmentation
Data augmentation [66] is a crucial preprocessing step aimed at expanding the diver-
sity of training samples, mitigating class imbalance, and enhancing model robustness. In 
MER, the challenge arises from the heterogeneous nature of multimodal inputs, where 
textual, acoustic, visual, and motion-based features exhibit different statistical proper-
ties. Augmentation strategies are applied across modalities to enhance the representa-
tional richness of the dataset while preserving emotional integrity.
A fundamental challenge in MER is the presence of emotion class imbalance, 
where certain emotions appear more frequently than others in naturalistic data-
sets. For instance, emotions such as neutral and happiness are overrepresented, 
while frustration, excitement, and anger occur less frequently. This imbalance 
skews model training, as classifiers tend to overfit to dominant emotions, leading to 
suboptimal recognition performance for minority classes.
To counteract this issue, Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) [67] are 
employed to synthesize additional training samples for underrepresented emotional 
categories. GANs operate by learning the latent distribution of emotional features and 
generating new, realistic samples that enhance the dataset’s diversity. The generator 
network creates synthetic samples, while the discriminator assesses their authenticity, 
refining the quality of generated data through adversarial learning. This augmentation

Comparative performance evaluation against state‑of‑the‑art methods
To establish the robustness and practical viability of the proposed MER system, a thor-
ough comparative analysis was performed against a wide array of recent state-of-the-
art models across benchmark datasets—namely IEMOCAP and MELD. As detailed in

sistent preprocessing, input representations, and evaluation metrics, thereby ensuring 
fairness and reproducibility.
The proposed architecture achieved near-perfect classification accuracies of 99.82% 
on IEMOCAP and 99.81% on MELD, along with identical macro- and weighted-average 
F1-scores. These results surpass all existing benchmarks in the literature, where the best-
performing models, such as [13, 14], and [80], report performance ceilings of approxi-
mately 73% and 66% on IEMOCAP and MELD, respectively. This dramatic leap of over 
25–30 percentage points in absolute accuracy signifies not only statistical superiority but 
also a paradigm shift in how multimodal emotional signals can be processed and inte-
grated for real-world affective computing systems.
From a methodological perspective, the observed improvements can be attributed to 
several interlocking innovations embedded in the proposed framework. First, the use of 
hierarchical attention-based GNNs allows the model to encode both intra- and inter-
modality relationships with structured precision, an aspect overlooked in many existing 
models that treat modality fusion as a flat or late-stage operation. Second, the incor-
poration of cross-modality transformers facilitates dynamic and context-aware interac-
tion across modalities, enabling adaptive weighting based on momentary salience. Third, 
contrastive learning with prototypical anchors introduces a self-supervised signal that 
enhances class boundary learning even in the presence of overlapping or ambiguous 
emotional states.

small-scale, noise-prone settings.
To further assess zero-shot generalization across linguistic and cultural domains, the 
system was evaluated on the CMU-MOSEAS dataset comprising Spanish, Portuguese, 
German, and French samples. Despite the absence of multilingual training, the model

contrastive learning and cross-modal transformer-based fusion.
Moreover, in the context of big data, the model’s low computational overhead (aver-

advantageous. This ensures suitability for real-time emotion-aware systems such as 
socially intelligent robots, empathetic virtual assistants, and multimodal behavioral 
monitoring platforms operating at scale. Such low-latency and high-throughput charac-
teristics address the pressing need for responsive and adaptive systems in high-velocity, 
high-volume environments.
In contrast, many existing models either (a) focus on a limited subset of modalities 
(e.g., text or audio only), (b) fail to scale computationally due to complex fusion archi-
tectures, or (c) lack robustness when confronted with non-stationary data streams. For 
example, models like [14, 18] rely heavily on manually designed fusion heuristics or 
adversarial alignment, which are less effective in diverse and dynamic settings. Others, 
such as CNN-based or LSTM-only models, fail to capture the hierarchical and relational 
structure of multimodal interactions.

Limitations and future work
Despite achieving strong empirical performance and real-time efficiency, the proposed 
MER framework has several limitations that open avenues for future research: 
1.	 Model Complexity vs. Edge Deployment: While ONNX optimization enables low-
latency inference (0.5 ms), the system still relies on high-capacity components such 
as transformer encoders and spatiotemporal fusion blocks. This poses challenges for 
deployment on resource-constrained devices. Future work will explore compression 
techniques—such as pruning, quantization, and knowledge distillation—to maintain 
accuracy while reducing runtime overhead.
2.	 Cultural and Sensor Generalization: The model’s generalization across cultural and 
linguistic boundaries remains limited, despite evaluation on a multilingual data-
set (CMU-Moseas). Variations in emotional expression across demographics and 
inconsistencies in sensor hardware (e.g., camera quality, microphone sensitivity) 
can degrade performance. Future directions include dataset diversification, domain 
adaptation, and sensor-invariant representation learning.
3.	 Limited Model Explainability: Although attention mechanisms offer some interpret-
ability, the framework lacks dedicated post-hoc explainability tools. In high-stakes or 
sensitive applications, transparent decision-making is crucial. We plan to integrate 
explainable AI (XAI) methods such as SHAP, Grad-CAM, and prototype-based visu-
alizations to enhance trust and model accountability.
To address these limitations, future work should include the following directions:
•	 Expand datasets to include low-resource languages, culturally specific expressions, 
and underrepresented demographics (e.g., SEWA, EmoReact, GEIC).
•	 Investigate domain generalization and unsupervised domain adaptation techniques 
to improve robustness across unseen cultural and sensor distributions.
•	 Incorporate fairness-aware objectives and subgroup analysis to ensure demographic 
equity.
•	 Develop sensor-agnostic learning modules to enable consistent performance across 
diverse hardware.
•	 Integrate advanced XAI techniques (e.g., SHAP, Grad-CAM, graph-based explainers) 
for modality-level transparency and ethical alignment.

Conclusion
This paper presents a robust framework for MER, integrating advanced machine learn-
ing techniques to enhance both the accuracy and efficiency of emotion prediction in 
dynamic, real-world contexts. By combining hierarchical attention-based graph neural 
networks (HAN-GNN), cross-modality transformer fusion (XMTF), and contrastive 
learning (CL), the proposed system achieves significant improvements over traditional 
emotion recognition methods. The system demonstrates impressive performance on 
benchmark datasets, such as MELD and IEMOCAP, where it excels in accuracy, recall, 
precision, F1-score, and AUC, effectively distinguishing complex emotional expressions 
across diverse modalities.
The proposed system’s success lies in its ability to seamlessly handle multimodal 
inputs—text, audio, video, and motion. The integration of modality-specific preprocess-
ing pipelines ensures optimal feature extraction for each data stream, while deep learn-
ing architectures such as HAN-GNN and XMTF allow for effective fusion, leading to 
improved emotion prediction accuracy and generalization. These results demonstrate 
the power of integrating multimodal data and advanced learning techniques to address 
the challenges posed by the variety and complexity inherent in big data for emotion rec-
ognition tasks.
Additionally, the model exhibits remarkable computational efficiency, with rapid 
convergence during batch training and low-latency inference during deployment. This 
efficiency is crucial for real-time applications, particularly in dynamic environments 
where quick decision-making is necessary, such as in HCI and healthcare applications. 
By leveraging advanced optimization strategies, the model successfully balances com-
putational demands with high performance, showcasing its potential for deployment in 
large-scale, real-time emotion recognition systems.
The framework also demonstrates robustness to noisy environments and cross-lin-
guistic generalization, as evidenced by its evaluation on the CMU-MOSEAS dataset, 
which spans multiple languages (Spanish, Portuguese, German, and French). This con-
firms the model’s capacity to generalize beyond English-based benchmarks, highlighting 
its potential for multilingual and cross-cultural deployment in global settings.
While the prior section has discussed in depth the limitations concerning model com-
plexity, cultural variability, and limited explainability, these remain important considera-
tions. Future extensions should focus on advancing explainable AI integration, fairness 
across demographic subgroups, and lightweight model variants for deployment on 
resource-constrained devices.
Overall, this research underscores the significant potential of MER systems to advance 
the field of affective computing. By addressing the challenges of big data variety and 
modality integration, the proposed framework contributes to more context-sensitive 
and accurate human-computer interactions. It’s demonstrated generalization across

Abstract: Emotion recognition in dynamic and real-world environments presents significant challenges due to the complexity and variability of multimodal data. This paper intro- duces an innovative Multimodal Emotion Recognition (MER) framework that seam- lessly integrates text, audio, video, and motion data using advanced machine learning techniques. To address challenges such as class imbalance, the framework employs Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for synthetic sample generation and Dynamic Prompt Engineering (DPE) for enhanced feature extraction across modalities. Text features are processed with Mistral-7B, audio with HuBERT, video with TimeSformer and LLaVA, and motion with MediaPipe Pose. The system efficiently fuses these inputs using Hierarchical Attention-based Graph Neural Networks (HAN-GNN) and Cross- Modality Transformer Fusion (XMTF), further improved by contrastive learning with Prototypical Networks to enhance class separation. The framework demonstrates exceptional performance, achieving training accuracies of 99.92% on IEMOCAP and 99.95% on MELD, with testing accuracies of 99.82% and 99.81%, respectively. High precision, recall, and specificity further highlight the robustness of the model. While trained on batch-processed datasets, the framework has been optimized for real-time applications, demonstrating computational efficiency with training completed in just 5 min and inference times under 0.4 ms per sample. This makes the system well- suited for real-time emotion recognition tasks despite being trained on batch data. It also generalizes effectively to noisy and multilingual settings, achieving strong results on SAVEE and CMU-MOSEAS, thereby confirming its resilience in diverse real-world scenarios. This research advances the field of MER, offering a scalable and efficient solution for affective computing. The findings emphasize the importance of refining these systems for real-world applications, particularly in complex, multimodal big data environments.
